standard.title: Health and wellbeing behaviours
standard.description: investigate and apply behaviours that contribute to their own and others' health, safety, relationships and wellbeing
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have investigated health messages and practices in their community and discussed their purposes (AC9HP2P06) and identified and demonstrated protective behaviours (AC9HP2P05). They understand health messages and basic safety behaviours but have not yet investigated or applied the full range of health behaviours across nutrition, physical activity, mental health and safety.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate and apply behaviours that contribute to their own and others' health, safety, relationships and wellbeing.

nodes.label: Safe storage of medications and substances
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how medications and other substances can be stored safely in the home and at school.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two safety rules for storing medications or substances safely and explain why each rule matters.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate how different types of substances (medications, cleaning products, personal care items) require safe storage, and explain the safety rationale for each.
wider: Examine how household product labelling conveys safety storage information (e.g. 'keep out of reach of children', 'store below 25°C') and investigate what happens when storage instructions are not followed.
Explore how schools manage medication storage for students and discuss the safety procedures involved.

response_modes.reason: Safe storage rules are best understood when the risk-consequence logic is explicit: 'we store it this way because if we didn't, X could happen'. Connecting rules to consequences builds more durable health and safety understanding than rule-memorisation alone.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two rules for safely storing medications or substances.
Explains the reason for at least one rule.
Applies the rules to identify a safe storage scenario.

nodes.label: Nutrition and healthy eating patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore the benefits of eating patterns that reflect the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and investigate nutritional information about foods.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the main food groups in the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating and describe at least one benefit of eating a variety of foods from different groups.
nodes.typical_width: Explore how eating patterns aligned with the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating contribute to health; investigate nutritional information on food labels or in food databases; discuss choices and their health implications.
wider: Compare their own typical daily food intake against the Guide to Healthy Eating recommendations and identify areas of alignment and areas for change.
Investigate nutritional information from a range of foods and examine what information on food labels (ingredients, nutrients, serving sizes) is most useful for making healthy choices.

response_modes.reason: Nutrition understanding deepens when students connect the Guide to Healthy Eating to real food contexts — their own eating, school canteen offerings, food labelling, and cultural food practices. Broad context exposure makes the recommendations tangible.

success_criteria: Names the main food groups in the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating.
Describes at least one health benefit associated with eating from each food group.
Reads basic nutritional information from a food label or database.

nodes.label: Mental health, belonging and connection
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss the importance of a sense of belonging and connection in promoting mental health and wellbeing.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe what belonging and connection mean and explain how they contribute to mental health and wellbeing.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how belonging and connection in different contexts (family, school, community, sport) promote mental health; identify actions individuals and groups can take to strengthen connection.
wider: Investigate how physical activity participation contributes to social connection and belonging, and explore examples where sport or community activity has improved wellbeing.
Explore mindfulness and meditation practices as mental health strategies, practising at least one technique regularly and reflecting on its effects.

response_modes.reason: The link between belonging, connection and mental health is not intuitive for primary students — it requires explicit concept building. A concrete discussion of what it feels like to belong (and not to belong) grounds the abstract mental health relationship.

success_criteria: Explains what 'belonging' and 'connection' mean in their own words.
Describes how belonging or connection affects a person's mental health.
Identifies one action they could take to strengthen belonging in their class or community.

nodes.label: Sustainability and health behaviours
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate ways to change their behaviours to support both their own health and the sustainability of the Earth's systems.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one behaviour change that would benefit both their health and the environment (e.g. choosing sustainable, healthy foods; reducing food waste; active transport).
nodes.typical_width: Investigate multiple health behaviours that also support sustainability — food choices, waste reduction, active transport, school gardens — discussing how individual actions connect to broader environmental and community health.
wider: Design and implement a small sustainability and health project (e.g. a classroom composting system or school garden contribution) and reflect on its health, social and environmental benefits.
Investigate how community fruit and vegetable gardens support both health and sustainability — exploring examples from Australian communities including First Nations food practices.

response_modes.reason: This node connects personal health behaviours (nutrition, activity) with environmental responsibility — an integration that requires students to hold both domains simultaneously. Explicit 'dual-benefit' framing (good for me AND good for the environment) supports the integration.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Sustainability-health connections are a genuinely rich and multidimensional exploration space — food systems, active transport, school gardens, and environmental health all offer distinct and meaningful investigations that widen understanding beyond individual health behaviour.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one behaviour that benefits both their health and the environment.
Explains the health benefit and the environmental benefit of that behaviour.
Proposes one realistic change they could make to a current habit.
